message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can easily check your own download/upload speeds with a quick command (or a web‑based test).  
Below are two common approaches you can try on a Windows machine:

---

## 1. Use **speedtest‑cli** (Python‑based)

If you have Python and `pip` installed, you can run a lightweight command‑line speed test.

```powershell
# 1️⃣ Install the tool (if you haven’t already)
pip install speedtest-cli

# 2️⃣ Run a simple test that prints download, upload, and ping
speedtest-cli --simple
```

**What you’ll see:**

```
Ping: 12.34 ms
Download: 123.45 Mbit/s
Upload: 67.89 Mbit/s
```

> *Tip:* If you want a more detailed report, drop the `--simple` flag and let the script output all the extra metrics.

---

## 2. Use the official Speedtest website (no installation)

If you prefer a browser‑based test, just open your favorite browser and go to:

- https://www.speedtest.net

Click “Go” and the site will automatically ping a nearby server, then download/upload a test file to give you the same three numbers (Ping, Download, Upload).

---

### Quick sanity check (optional)

If you just want to see that your network is up and you’re getting a decent ping, you can run:

```powershell
ping www.google.com -n 5
```

This will show you the round‑trip time (latency) for 5 packets. It won’t give you bandwidth, but it’s a good quick sanity check.

---

### What to do next

- **If you see very low download/upload numbers** (e.g., < 10 Mbit/s) or high latency (> 100 ms), contact your ISP or check your router/modem.
- **If the numbers look good** but you’re still experiencing slowness, the issue might be with a specific application or device on your network.

Let me know if you run into any trouble installing or running the test!
